rules.title: Baseline and functional unit before comparing
rules.what: Any resource comparison starts from a recorded baseline of the current alternative, measured on a stated functional unit.
rules.why: Without a baseline, 'faster' or 'lighter' means 'feels like it'. Comparisons without a unit compare different things.
rules.how: Record: task measured, workload, hardware/cloud context, method, sample size, uncertainty. Then measure the candidate the same way.

verify.how: A comparison ships with both measurements, same unit, same context, stated sample.

limits: No measurement means unknown gains, not zero impact.

rules.title: A tool score is an indicator, not compliance
rules.what: Never convert an EcoIndex, Lighthouse score, sonar score or a clean scan into 'RGESN/RGAA compliant'. Each tool proves only its narrow checks.
rules.why: Scores are proxies: they measure what they can measure, not what the referential requires. Treating a proxy as proof blocks the real audit and misleads the reader.
rules.how: Report the score with the tool name, version and date, next to what it does and does not cover. Compliance claims require the referential's own procedure.

verify.how: No compliance wording appears without the referential's test procedure and evidence.

rules.title: Distinguish technical gain from environmental impact
rules.what: Report technical gains as technical gains. An environmental claim requires a measured reduction on a stated boundary, and nothing else.
rules.why: Fewer bytes, less CPU, fewer tokens are real savings, but energy, water and CO2 depend on hardware, grid mix, caching and usage patterns. The direction is honest; the ratio must be measured.
rules.how: Say 'reduced transferred bytes by 40% (measured)', not 'reduced carbon footprint by 40%'. Never copy a percentage from a vendor, benchmark or case study.

verify.how: Every environmental wording in the docs traces to a measurement of its own.

limits: Direction of improvement (fewer resources processed -> less energy) holds qualitatively; the quantitative claim does not.

rules.title: Unknown is not zero
rules.what: When a gain was not measured, say 'unknown'; never present an unmeasured change as neutral or beneficial.
rules.why: 'Unknown' is actionable: it names the next measurement. 'Probably fine' hides both risks and wasted effort.
rules.how: In reports, mark each assessed rule verified / failed / not_tested / manual_review_required, and list measurement gaps as next actions.

verify.how: Reports contain an explicit measurement-gaps section.

rules.title: Monitor what grows
rules.what: Watch the resources that grow silently: payload sizes, query counts per view, cache sizes, log volumes, dependency counts, build times.
rules.why: Growth is invisible per change and obvious over a quarter. A budget alert catches what no single review can.
rules.how: Track the metric over time, set a budget per functional unit, alert when crossed, review the trend at each ecodesign review.

verify.how: Metric history exists with a budget and alert configuration.

limits: Monitoring itself costs; instrument the few metrics that drive decisions.

rules.title: State the method when you measure energy
rules.what: For material performance or energy changes, record the workload, duration, hardware or cloud context, tool, method and uncertainty, and say whether a value is metered, modelled or a proxy.
rules.why: Without the method, a figure cannot be reproduced or compared; a profiler or sampler alone measures one component, not the service.
rules.how: Follow references/measurement.md; label each number (metered / modelled / proxy); keep raw data with the result.

verify.how: The reported figure carries its method, context and uncertainty.
